parts: Lesson 2: Introduction to Mass Communication — Summary

The simplest definition of mass communication is 'public communication transmitted electronically or mechanically'. Messages are sent to large, perhaps millions or billions of people through mass media such as newspapers, magazines, films, radio, television and the internet. Media is the plural of medium, 'means of communication', also called the channel of communication. Mass communication can be defined as 'who' (communicator) 'says what' (message) 'in which channel' (medium) 'to whom' (receiver) 'with what effect' (impact of the message, e.g. a change of attitude towards dowry).

The functions of media are to inform (news bulletins), educate (a doctor speaking on prevention of disease, experts telling farmers about new seeds) and entertain (films, serials, music programmes). Examples of effect: the Green Revolution (radio told farmers to use the right seed and fertilizers), small family norm and the polio campaign ('Do boond zindagi ki').

Mass communication is a 20th century development. Men on horseback and pigeons carried messages; Kalidasa's Meghdoot used clouds as messenger. Paper (the Chinese used it in 105 AD; the word comes from papyrus), printing (Johannes Gutenberg of Germany, about 1439), newspapers, the telegraph (Samuel Morse, 1835; International Morse Code 1851), the telephone (Alexander Graham Bell, 1876), radio (Marconi, 1901), the transistor (1947, which made radio the most popular medium) and television (Baird, 1920) were the steps. Newspapers have limitations of time and need literate readers; the radio was the first truly mass medium.

Newspapers and journalism (first published in the 17th century in Germany, Italy and the Netherlands; in India Raja Rammohan Roy, Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Mahatma Gandhi used journalism in the freedom movement; Gandhiji started Indian Opinion in 1903 in South Africa, Harijan and wrote for Young India). Wireless communication (the cell phone). Photography (Niepce and Daguerre of France, 19th century). Films (Edison in the USA and the Lumiere brothers in France; talkies in 1927; the first Indian motion picture Raja Harishchandra by Dadasaheb Phalke; first Indian talkie Alam Ara). Radio (first formal radio station in Bombay; radio in India by the 1920s). Television (Baird, 1920; started in India in 1959 on an experimental basis, first station in Delhi; colour in 1982; satellite TV from early 1990s and DTH). New media (computers, information technology, communication networks and digital media) bring convergence, the coming together of many media forms. Traditional media are rooted in oral tradition and culture (story telling, folk songs, street theatre, puppetry, Ram Lila); performers and audience know each other and people never tire of them.
